entry.name: Stethoscope
entry.desc: The stethoscope is a medical device for listening to the sounds of the heart, lungs and intestines and to blood flow, a practice called auscultation. René Laennec invented it in 1816 at the Necker-Enfants Malades Hospital in Paris: a monaural wooden tube, devised after he found that a rolled piece of paper carried heart sounds without his ear touching the patient's chest. Golding Bird described one with a flexible tube in 1840, and Arthur Leared made a binaural stethoscope in 1851. George Philip Cammann's design of the following year, with a plug for each ear, has remained essentially unchanged since.

notes: civ left empty: France in 1816 (the Bourbon Restoration) has no profile; the Kingdom of France profile ends in 1792 and French Empire is the colonial empire. No parent on the tree fits (the ear trumpet it resembled is not a node).

entry.name: Blood transfusion
entry.desc: Blood transfusion is the transfer of blood or its components into the veins of a human or other animal. The physician Richard Lower performed the first reliably documented successful transfusion, between two dogs, in February 1665, and described it to the Royal Society that December. On 15 June 1667 Jean-Baptiste Denys transfused a sheep's blood into a 15-year-old boy, but deaths after such experiments led to bans in 1668. James Blundell performed the first successful transfusion of human blood, for bleeding after childbirth, in 1818 at Guy's Hospital in London, and Karl Landsteiner's discovery of blood groups in 1901 gave the practice a scientific basis.

row.label: Blood transfusion
row.contested: Lower's transfusion was between two dogs; the first from an animal to a human was Jean-Baptiste Denys's in France in 1667, and the first successful one of human blood James Blundell's in London in 1818.

notes: Dated to Lower's dog-to-dog transfusion of February 1665, which the article calls the first reliably documented successful transfusion. The article does not say where it was done (only that Lower was working at the Royal Society, and that his London transfusion of 1667 was the first of its kind in Britain), so place is just 'Britain'. civ Kingdom of England is inferred from Britain and the Royal Society, not named in the article: drop it if that is too loose. Parent de-motu-cordis: the article says recorded research into transfusion began with William Harvey's experiments on the circulation. abo-blood-group-system (1901) is later and cannot be a parent.

entry.name: Prosthesis
entry.desc: A prosthesis is an artificial device that replaces a missing body part lost through injury, disease or a condition present at birth. The earliest archaeological evidence is an eye prosthesis, probably of bitumen paste covered with a thin layer of gold, buried with a woman at Shahr-i Shōkhta in Iran about 3000 to 2800 BCE. A wood and leather artificial big toe found on a mummy near Thebes, dated 950 to 710 BCE, shows signs of use. Ambroise Paré, considered the father of modern prosthetics, designed an above-knee device, and functional prostheses appeared in the 1500s.

row.label: Prosthesis
row.contested: The wood and leather toe from a burial near Thebes, dated 950 to 710 BCE, is described as the first confirmed use of a prosthetic device, as it shows wear; before its discovery in 2000 the oldest known was an artificial leg from Capua.

notes: The article is inconsistent: it calls the Shahr-i Shokhta eye (c. 3000-2800 BC) 'the earliest archaeological evidence of prosthetics' and the Theban toe (950-710 BC) 'the first confirmed use of a prosthetic device'. I dated the node to the eye (the earliest evidence the article accepts) and put the toe in contested; the editor may prefer -950 if 'confirmed use' should rule. The Eye of Horus story and the Rigveda's Vishpala are myth or text and left out. No profile for Shahr-i Shokhta; civ empty. 'Iran' is in the article ('ancient Iran').

entry.name: Sulfonamide
entry.desc: Sulfonamides, or sulfa drugs, were the first broadly effective antibacterial medicines used systemically. Experiments began in 1932 in the laboratories of Bayer AG, then part of IG Farben, where a team led by Gerhard Domagk found that Prontosil, a red dye synthesised by Josef Klarer, stopped some bacterial infections in mice; the first report appeared in 1935. A team at the Pasteur Institute showed that the body breaks Prontosil down into sulfanilamide, a compound first made in 1906 whose patent had expired. Between 1937 and 1943 sulfa drugs lowered maternal mortality in the United States by 25–40%.

row.label: Sulfa drugs
row.contested: Domagk's team found the drug, but its active compound, sulfanilamide, had been synthesised in 1906 and used in dye-making; a French team at the Pasteur Institute showed that Prontosil works by releasing it in the body.

notes: Type term with no subtype, as the existing drug entries (penicillin, aspirin, insulin). The article gives no city for Bayer's laboratories, so place is 'Bayer AG laboratories'. civ weimar-republic (an entry; no German profile is alive in 1932) rests only on the article's 'German chemical trust' and 'German corporation': drop it if too loose. Parent synthetic-dye: the Bayer team worked from coal-tar dyes and Prontosil was a dye. The elixir sulfanilamide disaster of 1937 (at least 100 poisoned) is left out of the desc for length.

entry.name: Artificial cardiac pacemaker
entry.desc: An artificial cardiac pacemaker is a medical device that sends electrical pulses through electrodes to the chambers of the heart to keep an even heart rate. The first fully implantable pacemaker, designed by the inventor Rune Elmqvist and the surgeon Åke Senning, was implanted on 8 October 1958 at the Karolinska Institute in Solna, Sweden; it failed after three hours, and its patient, Arne Larsson, went on to receive 26 pacemakers. Earlier devices were external, from Mark C Lidwill's apparatus of 1926 in Sydney to John Hopps's of 1950. Wilson Greatbatch's lithium iodide cell of 1971 led to pacemakers lasting up to eleven years.

row.label: Cardiac pacemaker
row.contested: Mark C Lidwill's portable apparatus of 1926 in Sydney already paced the heart from outside the body, and Albert Hyman called his hand-cranked instrument of 1932 an artificial pacemaker; the first implanted one dates from 1958.

notes: The saved article's title is 'Pacemaker' (the target of Artificial cardiac pacemaker); source given as 'Pacemaker'. The article defines a pacemaker as an implanted device, so the node is dated to the first implantation (1958); the external pacing apparatus of 1926 (Lidwill) and 1932 (Hyman, who coined the term) are in contested. Parent transistor: the article calls the silicon transistor's availability in 1956 the pivotal event for practical pacemaking (it does not say Elmqvist's device used one). voltaic-pile (electric battery) as the power source. 'eleven years': the article says 'from one year to as long as eleven years'.

entry.name: Organ transplantation
entry.desc: Organ transplantation is the removal of an organ or tissue from one body and its placement in another, to replace a damaged or missing function. The first transplant in the modern sense was performed in 1883 by the Swiss surgeon Theodor Kocher, who reversed the symptoms that followed the complete removal of the thyroid by implanting thyroid tissue. Alexis Carrel's techniques for joining blood vessels, from the early 1900s, laid the groundwork for later transplant surgery, but rejection defeated most attempts until Joseph Murray's kidney transplant between identical twins in Boston in 1954. Christiaan Barnard performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in 1967.

row.label: Organ transplant
row.contested: Skin grafts are older: Sushruta used grafted skin to rebuild noses in the 2nd century BCE. The first successful kidney transplant is given as Joseph Murray's in Boston in 1954, though a timeline of transplants lists one by Richard H. Lawler in Chicago in 1950.

notes: Dated to Kocher's thyroid transplant of 1883, which the article calls 'the first transplant in the modern sense' and 'the first organ transplant'. The article does not name the city, so place is 'Switzerland' (in the article's timeline) and civ Swiss Confederation follows from 'Swiss surgeon'. The article contradicts itself on the first successful kidney transplant (1954 Murray in the text, 1950 Lawler in its timeline): in contested. Sushruta is dated '2nd century BC' here, while the tree's sushruta-samhita node is 300: worth a look. Parents general-anaesthesia and antiseptic-surgery are not named by the article; I took the dependence of an 1883 organ operation on both as plain: drop them if not. Apocryphal accounts (Pien Chi'ao, Cosmas and Damian) left out.

entry.name: Electric motor
entry.desc: An electric motor is a machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, usually through the interaction of a magnetic field and the current in a wire winding. Michael Faraday first showed electromagnetic rotation on 3 September 1821 at the Royal Institution, where a wire carrying a current turned around a magnet in a pool of mercury. Ányos Jedlik built a device with a stator, rotor and commutator in 1828, William Sturgeon a DC motor able to turn machinery in 1832, and Frank Julian Sprague the first practical DC motor in 1886. Galileo Ferraris and Nikola Tesla invented AC induction motors in 1885 and 1887.

row.label: Electric motor
row.contested: Andrew Gordon and Benjamin Franklin described electrostatic motors in the 1740s and 1750s, but these were never put to practical use; Faraday's device of 1821 was the first electromagnetic one.

notes: 'London' is not in the article, so place is 'Royal Institution'. civ empty, as on the tree's electromagnetic-induction and electric-generator rows for Faraday. Ferraris (1885) and Tesla (1887) invented their induction motors independently, as the article says; not put in 'also', since they are a later kind (AC), not an independent origin of the motor.

entry.name: Diesel engine
entry.desc: A diesel engine is an internal combustion engine in which the fuel is ignited by the heat of air compressed in the cylinder, without a spark plug. The German engineer Rudolf Diesel published his idea in 1893 in Theory and Construction of a Rational Heat Motor, and his first prototype was built that summer at the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg, with the first ignition on 10 August 1893. A redesigned engine ran for 88 revolutions in February 1894, and the third prototype, tested on 17 February 1897, reached an effective efficiency of 26.2%, against the 6–10% of steam engines that Diesel had learned of as a student.

row.label: Diesel engine
row.contested: Critics, among them Otto Köhler and Emil Capitaine, claimed that Diesel had invented nothing new; Capitaine lost a patent lawsuit against him. Diesel may have taken the idea of air-blast injection from George B. Brayton.

notes: civ German Empire follows from 'German engineer' and Augsburg in 1893; the article does not name the state. Parent steam-engine: Diesel set out to beat the steam engine's 6-10% efficiency (Linde's lectures, 1878); drop it if only direct technical ancestors are wanted.

entry.name: Hydroelectricity
entry.desc: Hydroelectricity is electricity generated from hydropower, the energy of moving water. Water had long driven machinery, but the first hydroelectric power scheme was developed in 1878 by William Armstrong at Cragside in Northumberland, England, where it powered a single arc lamp in his art gallery. The Schoelkopf Power Station No. 1 near Niagara Falls began to produce electricity in 1881, and by 1889 there were 200 hydroelectric power stations in the United States alone. Dams grew larger through the 20th century, to the Three Gorges Dam in China at 22.5 GW, and hydropower supplied 15% of the world's electricity in 2023.

row.label: Hydroelectricity
civ: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

notes: civ follows from England in 1878 (the article names no state). Parents: water-wheel (the article traces hydropower to mechanical use), electric-generator ('the electrical generator was developed and could now be coupled with hydraulics'), and incandescent-light-bulb (the tree's 'Electric light', 1802: Cragside's scheme lit an arc lamp). No entry for William Armstrong, so '=William Armstrong'.

entry.name: Alternating current
entry.desc: Alternating current is an electric current that periodically reverses direction, the form in which electric power is delivered to homes and businesses. The French instrument maker Hippolyte Pixii built the first alternator to produce it in 1832, on Michael Faraday's principles. In 1885 Károly Zipernowsky, Ottó Bláthy and Miksa Déri of the Ganz Works in Budapest patented closed-core transformers, and their system of 75 transformers supplied 1,067 lamps at the Hungarian National Exhibition that May. Westinghouse then built AC systems across the United States, and the first three-phase system was established in Frankfurt in 1891.

row.label: Alternating current
row.contested: Pixii's alternator came first, but alternating current became practical for power only with the transformers of the 1880s; from late 1887 Thomas Edison campaigned against it as too dangerous in the war of the currents.

notes: Dated to Pixii's alternator of 1832, the first to produce alternating current. The article gives no place (only 'French instrument maker'), so place and civ are empty (no French profile fits 1832 anyway). The node could instead be dated to the first AC power systems (Ganz Works, Budapest, 1878-1885): the editor's choice. Type work/other (a form of power supply rather than a device): change to idea/concept if preferred.

entry.name: Lithium-ion battery
entry.desc: A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery that stores energy by moving lithium ions in and out of electronically conducting solids. M. Stanley Whittingham conceived intercalation electrodes in the 1970s and made the first rechargeable lithium-ion battery, with a titanium disulfide cathode, though safety problems kept it from being commercialized. John Goodenough used lithium cobalt oxide as a cathode in 1980, and Akira Yoshino developed the first prototype of the modern battery, with a carbonaceous anode, in 1985. A Sony and Asahi Kasei team led by Yoshio Nishi brought it to market in 1991, and the three inventors shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

notes: The saved article's History section is empty (moved to its own article); everything comes from the lead. It gives only 'the 1970s' for Whittingham's battery and names no place or country (no Exxon, Oxford or Japan), so place and civ are empty; year 1970 with circa 1, as the tree does for decade dates (green-revolution 1940, '1940s'). If a firm year is wanted, 1985 (Yoshino's prototype of the modern battery) is the next date the article gives.

entry.name: Wind turbine
entry.desc: A wind turbine is a device that converts the kinetic energy of wind into electrical energy. The first to generate electricity was installed by the Austrian Josef Friedländer at the Vienna International Electrical Exhibition in 1883: a Halladay wind motor 6.6 m across, whose 3.7 kW drove a dynamo that charged batteries. James Blyth lit his holiday home in Marykirk, Scotland, with one in July 1887, and Charles F. Brush built the first automatically operated wind turbine some months later. A 100 kW forerunner of modern horizontal-axis machines ran at Yalta in 1931, and by 2024 turbines generated over 1,136 gigawatts.

row.label: Wind turbine
row.contested: Wind had powered machines since the windwheel of Hero of Alexandria and the vertical-axle windmills built in Sistan from the 7th century; Friedländer's machine of 1883 was the first to generate electricity.

notes: civ empty: no Austria-Hungary profile or entry exists. Parents: windmill, electric-generator (the dynamo) and voltaic-pile (the batteries it charged). For the editor: this article dates the Sistan vertical-axle windmills 'from the 7th century', while the tree's windmill node is 850 (9th century, Khorasan): the two articles differ.
